claims.text: High-entropy alloys are composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The initial nanoparticles form a single solid-solution phase verified by XRD and microscopy.
The synergy of high configurational entropy and moderate lattice distortion is the dominant factor securing nanoparticle stability from 473 to 1923 K.
High configurational entropy and moderate lattice distortion prevent substantial phase segregation or chemical ordering at elevated temperatures.
Mixing entropy favors formation and retention of a single-phase solid solution.
Moderate multi-element lattice distortion reduces the tendency for phase segregation as temperature varies.
Increasing temperature strengthens the configurational-entropy contribution relative to enthalpic driving forces for segregation or ordering.
The entropy contribution offsets the enthalpic driving force for elemental segregation and stabilizes a uniform solid solution.
From 473 to 1923 K, XRD will show only thermal-expansion peak shifts and no new phase reflections.
TEM elemental mapping will show uniform metal distributions across all particles up to 1923 K.
At 473 K, the nanoparticles have a single solid-solution phase and near-equimolar concentrations of five or more metals.
Large atomic-size mismatches can make lattice-distortion or entropy stabilization insufficient and permit phase decomposition.
Strong favorable mixing or ordering enthalpies can overcome entropic stabilization and promote chemical association or decomposition.
Stability under repeated thermal cycling or changes in partial pressure remains uncertain.
Evidence spanning the full 473–1923 K range is limited.
Detection of a new phase, nonuniform compositional regions, or pronounced morphology changes in the test nanoparticles would falsify the proposed stability mechanism.
